title: Create a focused context manager with contextlib
sources: Python 3.14 Standard Library: contextlib.contextmanager; Python 3.14 Language Reference: with statement; reviewed 2026-10-03
masterChecklist: Context managers and with; creating context managers where appropriate
whyItMatters: A short acquisition-and-cleanup rule should live in one place rather than be copied around every call site. For simple resource lifetimes, contextlib can express that rule without a separate class.
simpleExplanation: @contextmanager turns a generator function into a context manager. Code before its single yield runs on entry; the yielded value becomes the name after as; code after yield runs on exit. Put cleanup in finally so it happens if the with body raises. An error from the body is thrown back at the yield point. If you catch that error only to log it, re-raise it; otherwise the context manager may silently suppress it. A class with __enter__/__exit__ is often clearer when the manager has more state or reusable behavior.
mentalModel: Yield is the handoff point: the manager prepares the workspace, lends it to the with block, then takes it back and tidies it. A finally block makes that tidying unconditional.
outcomes: Write a one-yield contextmanager with try/finally.
Explain why the body error reaches the yield point.
Check cleanup on normal and error exits.
Avoid accidental suppression when logging an error.

realWorldExample.scenario: A study-import job sets an in-memory active flag while one batch runs.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: If a record conversion fails, a manually cleared flag may remain True and later runs may think an import is still active.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Own the active flag in one small context manager, clean it in finally, and let the caller decide how to handle the batch error.

explanation: The decorator makes the one-yield generator usable in with.
Before yield, the flag is set; the yielded mapping is the current variable inside the block.
The deliberately raised ValueError resumes the generator at yield as an exception, but finally still clears the flag.
The manager does not swallow the exception. The outer boundary handles it and confirms active is False.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Remove the deliberate raise and observe that the flag still clears after a normal exit. Do not remove finally from a real cleanup path.

procedure: Name one resource or temporary state and identify its owner.
Write a generator function with exactly one yield and decorate it with @contextmanager.
Acquire before yield and release in finally after yield.
Catch and re-raise inside the manager only if it truly needs to add context; otherwise let the error propagate.
Test both normal and exceptional with bodies.

commonMistakes.why: The protocol expects exactly one handoff for a single with use.
commonMistakes.avoid: Keep one yield with setup before and cleanup after.

commonMistakes.mistake: Catching the body error for logging but not re-raising it.
commonMistakes.why: That can make a failed operation appear successful.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use finally for cleanup, or re-raise after logging.

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting cleanup only on the normal path after yield.
commonMistakes.why: An exception thrown into the generator can skip ordinary following statements.

lab.title: Make a temporary in-memory run flag
lab.safety: The exercise changes only a fictional dictionary and raises a local practice error.
guidedSteps: Set state['active'] to True before yielding.
Add try: yield state followed by finally that resets the flag.
Check that the outer except sees the error but the flag is False afterward.
checks: Output lines are True, False, True, caught, False.
Cleanup runs on both paths and the error remains visible to the outer handler.
lab.solutionExplanation: The decorator controls entry and exit around one yield. finally clears the state after either body outcome; the ValueError propagates to the outer except.
challenges: Predict the output if the failing branch is removed.
Find the bug: except ValueError: print('failed') inside the manager without re-raising.
Experiment: use two separate state dictionaries and explain who owns each flag.

projectConnection.milestone: Use a narrow context-manager boundary for the active-run state and test both success and failure paths.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: The state is inactive after every run; unexpected body errors still reach the caller.

assessment.question: Where does code before yield run?
assessment.answer: On entry to the with block.
assessment.explanation: It prepares the managed state before the body receives it.

assessment.question: Why put cleanup in finally?
assessment.answer: So cleanup runs whether the with body succeeds or raises.
assessment.explanation: The body error is thrown back at the yield point.

assessment.question: What should a manager do after catching an error only to log it?
assessment.explanation: Otherwise the failed operation may be suppressed unintentionally.
